The alarm didn't go off. I woke up anyway because the light was doing that thing it does in late August when the sun is too polite to wait for curtains. It slipped in under the edge and laid itself across my face like a warm hand. I didn't move for a while. The ceiling had a crack that looks like a river if you squint. I have been squinting at it for three years and it never changes, which is comforting in a way that is hard to explain without sounding sentimental.

The apartment smells like the coffee I made last night and forgot to drink. It is cold now, with a skin on top. I drink it anyway because I am trying to be less wasteful and also because the bitterness feels honest. My phone is on the nightstand, face down. I flip it over and see three messages from people I love and one from a bank. The bank can wait. The others are just check-ins, nothing urgent. One says "morning". One sends a photo of a dog in a sweater. One says "thinking of you" with no context. I like that one the most.

I get up and my knees make a sound I pretend not to hear. The floor is cold. I go to the kitchen and the kettle is already half full from yesterday. I fill it again. While it heats I stand at the sink and watch the neighbor across the alley water his plants. He does it every morning at 7:12. He has a small blue watering can with a chipped spout. I have never seen him without a hat. Today he is wearing a red one.

The kettle whistles. I make tea instead of coffee because my stomach is still deciding what it wants to be. The mug is chipped on the rim. I bought it in a thrift store for two dollars and it has been my favorite ever since. It fits my hand exactly. I take it to the balcony and the air is cooler than it should be. There is a pigeon on the railing. It looks at me like I am an inconvenience. I think about how many pigeons have sat on that same railing and how none of them ever wrote a poem about it.

I have been writing a lot lately, or trying to. The page stays mostly blank. I open my notebook and the last line I wrote is from Tuesday: "Maybe the point is not to get anywhere." I read it three times and decide it is both true and useless. I write underneath: "Maybe the point is to keep going back to the kettle." That feels truer.

My mind drifts to the grocery store yesterday. The automatic doors sighed open and a woman in front of me was trying to get a child to wear a mask. The child was three and said no very clearly. The mother was exhausted. I wanted to help but I also wanted to be invisible. I bought apples that were slightly too soft and a bunch of cilantro that will wilt by Friday. I forgot bread.

There is a song playing from somewhere downstairs. Bass thumps through the floorboards. I can never tell which apartment it is. I hum along without knowing the words. The pigeon leaves. A delivery truck beeps as it reverses. The city is waking up in pieces.

I think about my father sometimes in the morning. He used to make pancakes on Sundays and burn the edges on purpose because he said the outside was the best part. He would tell me the same joke every week about the chicken who crossed the road and I would pretend I hadn't heard it. I miss that predictability. I miss the way he would hum while he cooked, off-key and happy.

I check the weather. Rain later. Good. I like rain for walking. I like the way it makes everyone move slower, like we are all in on a secret. I put on a sweater I have had since college. It has a small hole under the arm. I like it more now because of the hole. It is a map of where I have been.

My thoughts keep circling back to small things. The way the light hits the chipped mug. The way the neighbor's watering can catches sun for half a second. The way my phone buzzes in my pocket when I am trying to think of nothing. I want to be a person who can sit still. I am learning that stillness is not empty. It is full of the things I usually drown out.

The tea is lukewarm now. I drink it anyway. I think about writing something that matters. Then I think about the fact that I have already written three pages about a crack in the ceiling and a pigeon. Maybe that is enough. Maybe that is everything.

I go inside and start the day. The kettle is still warm. The bank message can wait until lunch. The dog in the sweater can live in my head for a while. I open the notebook again and write: "August 12. The sun came in early. The pigeon left. I am still here." It is not profound. It is accurate. I close the notebook and put it on the table. I will come back to it later, or I won't. Either way, the day has begun, and that is something.
